definitions.definition: (intransitive, used with "of") To eliminate or to get rid of something.
To distribute or arrange; to put in place.

quote.citation: 1599 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Life of Henry the Fift”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act IV, scene iii]:
quote.text: Now, dear soldiers, march away: / And how thou pleasest, God, dispose the day!

quote.citation: 1811, [Jane Austen], Sense and Sensibility […], volume (please specify |volume=I to III), London:  […]  C[harles] Roworth, […], and published by T[homas] Egerton, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: Marianne’s pianoforte was unpacked and properly disposed of, and Elinor’s drawing were affixed to the walls of their sitting rooms.

quote.citation: 1934, Rex Stout, Fer-de-Lance, Bantam, published 1992, →ISBN, page 47:
quote.text: I sat down within three feet of the entrance door, and I had no sooner got disposed than the door opened and a man came in […] .

quote.citation: 1950 September, “Central London Railway Jubilee”, in Railway Magazine, page 620:
quote.text: By disposing the driving power over a number of cars instead of concentrating it in a single locomotive a great advance was made towards a high rate of acceleration.

definitions.definition: To deal out; to assign to a use.

quote.citation: 1818 (first published), John Evelyn, diary entry for 1634
quote.text: what he designed to bestow on her funeral, he would rather dispose among the poor

quote.citation: 1697, Virgil, “(please specify the book number)”, in John Dryden, transl., The Works of Virgil: Containing His Pastorals, Georgics, and Æneis. […], London:  […]  Jacob Tonson, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: Endure and conquer; Jove will soon dispose / To future good our past and present woes.

quote.citation: 1625, Francis [Bacon], “Of Suspicion”, in The Essayes […], 3rd edition, London:  […]  Iohn Haviland for Hanna Barret, →OCLC:
quote.text: They [suspicions] dispose kings to tyranny, husbands to jealousy, and wise men to irresolution and melancholy.

quote.citation: 1892, Walter Besant, chapter II, in The Ivory Gate […], New York, N.Y.: Harper & Brothers, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: At twilight in the summer […] the mice come out. They […] eat the luncheon crumbs. Mr. Checkly, for instance, always brought his dinner in a paper parcel in his coat-tail pocket, and ate it when so disposed, sprinkling crumbs lavishly […] on the floor.

quote.citation: 1599 (first performance), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Iulius Cæsar”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act I, scene ii]:

definitions.definition: (obsolete) To regulate; to adjust; to settle; to determine.

quote.citation: 1700, [John] Dryden, “Palamon and Arcite: Or, The Knight’s Tale. In Three Books.”, in Fables Ancient and Modern; […], London:  […]  Jacob Tonson, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: the knightly forms of combat to dispose

definitions.definition: (obsolete) The disposal or management of something.

quote.citation: 1680, John Bunyan, The Life and Death of Mr Badman:
quote.text: By thus doing, he submits himself to God's rod, commits himself to the dispose of his providence; yea, by thus doing, he casteth the lot of his present and future condition into the lap of his creditors, and leaves the whole dispose thereof to the Lord  […]
